title: Partners
hookLine: the first fight about whose job the dishes are; the Sigalovada's five duties, both ways
tomorrow: can you love someone without holding on too tight?

cards: Wedding planning: the seating chart, the playlist, the signs.
And somewhere in there, the first real fight about whose job the dishes are going to be, and whose mother gets called on Sundays, and who keeps track of the bills. Small questions, carrying big ones.
So what do two partners owe each other? The Sigalovada, the same teaching that made parents the east, gives an answer in a short list, and it runs in both directions.

teach.b: In the Buddha's map for Sigala, the west is partner and children.
For the partners, he lays out five duties each way. The sutta was spoken to a young man, so it starts with him. He honors his wife.
He doesn't look down on her. He's faithful. He hands over authority in the home.
And he gives her gifts; the text says ornaments. Then hers. She does her work well.
She's kind to the relatives on both sides. She's faithful. She guards what they've earned.
And she's skilled and tireless at what she does.

An honest note: these words come from a world of fixed roles, and some of them land differently today. Couples today may divide the work differently, and the sutta doesn't settle that. What it does settle is the shape.
Faithfulness is on both lists. Respect runs one way as honor and the other as care for the family. Trust is handed over, authority to one, the household's earnings to the other.
Neither is only a giver or only a receiver.
Done that way, the sutta says, the west is covered, made safe and secure. Two people, each guarding a side of the same house. Not one guard and one guest.
And when they argue about who guards which side, that's not the house falling down. That's the duties being worked out, out loud, between people who both mean to keep them.

how: Some Buddhist wedding blessings and marriage talks draw on the Sigalovada's duties between partners; in some Buddhist communities marriage itself is a civil and family matter, and monks may be invited to chant blessings.

s: the Buddha taught only monks and had nothing to say about marriage
in the Sigalovada he gives a young householder five duties each way between partners.
in the Sigalovada, faithfulness is a duty of both partners
it appears on both lists of five.
the sutta settles exactly how a couple should split the housework
it comes from a world of fixed roles; what it settles is the shape: duties running both ways.

games.q: your older cousin is engaged. she says the old texts just make wives serve husbands. you've read the Sigalovada. what's the fair reply?
o: it has a husband's five duties too: honor, respect, faithfulness, trust, gifts.
she's right: the duties run only from the wife to the husband.
the text says partners owe each other nothing once they're married.
games.why: the sutta lists five duties each way. its roles come from its own world, but faithfulness and respect run in both directions.

practice: Bring to mind a partner, or anyone you share a life with: a roommate, a sibling, a friend. Choose one thing you'd like to do for them this week, and name what usually gets in the way.
Then picture the moment you'll do it anyway: when, where, and the first small step.

wordCard.voice: Partners: the west in the Sigalovada, in Pali pacchima disa, the western direction. Five duties each way, faithfulness on both lists.

orig.note: Pali: the western direction, which the Sigalovada gives to partner and children.

carryVoice: Here's the line: west, where two people guard one house from both sides. Four of eleven, on family.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 31 (Sigalovada Sutta: the west as wife and children; a husband ministers to his wife by honoring her, not disparaging her, being faithful, handing over authority, and providing adornments; a wife performs her duties well, is hospitable to the relatives, is faithful, guards his earnings, and is skilled and diligent; 'thus the west is covered, made safe and secure')
